chapter.name: Area
chapter.blurb: Area of a rectangle and square and why perimeter does not measure it; deriving the triangle area formula 1/2 x base x height via an enclosing rectangle and using it to prove equal-area results from a rectangle's diagonals, a triangle's median, and triangles between parallels; finding the area of any polygon by triangulation; dissecting a parallelogram, rhombus and trapezium into a rectangle to derive their area formulas, including the diagonal-product formula for a rhombus; and real-life area units and conversions.

scope_in.item: Area of a rectangle and a square as the count of unit squares covering it (Area = length x width; Area = side x side), and why the perimeter of a region does not determine its area
Deriving the area of a triangle by enclosing it in a rectangle: Area = 1/2 x base x height, shown to hold for right, acute and obtuse triangles, and using it to find an unknown base or height

Applications of the triangle area formula that compare areas without computing them: the four triangles formed by a rectangle's diagonals are equal in area, a median divides a triangle into two equal-area triangles, and triangles sharing a base between the same two parallel lines have equal area

Finding the area of any polygon by triangulation: splitting a quadrilateral along a diagonal into two triangles and adding their areas, and the general principle that any polygon (e.g. a pentagon or hexagon) can be divided into triangles
Deriving the area of a parallelogram by dissecting it into a rectangle: Area = base x height, using any side as the base with its matching perpendicular height

Area of a rhombus: since a rhombus is a parallelogram, base x height applies; the special formula Area = 1/2 x product of the diagonals, derived from the rhombus's diagonals bisecting each other at right angles

Deriving the area of a trapezium by dissection (breaking it into a rectangle and triangles, into a parallelogram and a triangle, or by joining two copies of it into a parallelogram): Area = 1/2 x height x sum of the parallel sides

Area units and conversions used in real life: 1 in = 2.54 cm, 1 ft = 12 in, 1 in2 = 6.4516 cm2, 1 acre = 43,560 ft2, and larger areas measured in m2 and km2, applied to estimating everyday areas such as an A4 sheet, a room or a plot of land

scope_out.item: The reflection/mirror-image proof that the minimum-perimeter triangle between two parallel lines with a common base is found using the perpendicular bisector
scope_out.reason: This is an exploratory 'Math Talk' investigation about minimum perimeter (pp. 156-157), not about area, and it is not restated in the chapter's own SUMMARY of what it taught

scope_out.item: The Sulba-Sutra and Euclid's Elements dissection problems posed as open-ended 'give a method' construction tasks, such as converting a rectangle into a triangle of equal area or an isosceles triangle into a rectangle
scope_out.reason: These are hands-on construction and investigation exercises inviting the reader's own method rather than a single computable factual answer; they are illustrative asides the chapter does not restate as a testable rule

scope_out.item: Numeric conversion factors for local area units such as bigha, gaj, katha, dhur, cent and ankanam
scope_out.reason: The chapter only names these as units that vary by region and asks the reader to find out the local one; no conversion factor for any of them is given in the book

scope_out.item: The actual areas of real cities, villages, towns, or the largest/smallest cities in India and the world
scope_out.reason: These are open 'find out' research prompts on p. 171 with no answer given in the chapter, not stated facts

scope_out.reason: These are blank grid and dot paper provided for hands-on cutting, folding and drawing activities, not chapter content with facts or formulas to test

concepts.name: Area of a rectangle and square, and why perimeter is not area
concepts.description: Measuring area by counting unit squares, the formula Area = length x width for a rectangle (and side squared for a square), and why the perimeter of a region does not determine its area.
concepts.idea: Area is the number of unit squares (or fractions of them) that cover a region; two regions can share a perimeter yet have different areas, so perimeter never measures area.
concepts.rule: Area of a rectangle = length x width; area of a square of side s = s x s. Two regions can have equal perimeters but different areas, and a region with a larger perimeter can have a smaller area than one with a smaller perimeter -- perimeter is not indicative of area.
concepts.example: A 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle and an 8 cm by 3 cm rectangle both have perimeter 22 cm, since 2x(7+4)=22 and 2x(8+3)=22, yet their areas are 28 cm2 and 24 cm2, which are different.

concepts.name: Area of a triangle: formula and derivation
concepts.description: Deriving the triangle area formula by enclosing a triangle in a rectangle, and showing the formula holds for every triangle, including obtuse ones.
concepts.idea: A triangle's area is half the area of a rectangle built on its base and height, so Area = half times base times height, for any triangle.
concepts.rule: Draw a rectangle around the triangle using its base and height (the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base or its extension). The triangle covers exactly half this rectangle, so Area of a triangle = 1/2 x base x height. For an obtuse triangle, where the foot of the perpendicular falls outside the base, the same formula is obtained as the difference of two right-triangle areas: Area(ABC) = 1/2 x h x DC - 1/2 x h x DB = 1/2 x h x BC.
concepts.example: A rectangle with sidelengths 7 cm and 4 cm is split by its diagonal into two triangles, each of area 1/2x7x4 = 14 cm2.

concepts.name: Equal-area results from the triangle area formula
concepts.description: Using the fact that a triangle's area depends only on its base and height to show, without computing either area, that certain pairs of triangles have equal area.
concepts.idea: Because area depends only on base and height, a rectangle's diagonals, a triangle's median, and triangles sharing a base between two parallel lines all produce triangles of provably equal area.
concepts.rule: The diagonals of a rectangle divide it into 4 triangles of equal area, since opposite triangles share equal bases (halves of the diagonals, which bisect each other) and the same height. A median (from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side) divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area, since they share equal bases and the same height from the opposite vertex. Triangles with the same base and third vertex on a line parallel to the base all have equal area, since they share the same base and the same perpendicular height.
concepts.example: In rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O, triangles AOB, BOC, COD and DOA all have equal area, each one-quarter of the rectangle.

concepts.name: Area of any polygon by triangulation
concepts.description: Finding the area of a quadrilateral or any polygon by splitting it into triangles and adding their areas.
concepts.idea: Any polygon can be divided into triangles, so once we know how to find a triangle's area, we can find the area of any polygon by adding up the triangles' areas.
concepts.rule: A diagonal of a quadrilateral divides it into two triangles; the sum of their areas is the quadrilateral's area. A pentagon can be divided into three triangles from one vertex, and in general any n-sided polygon can always be divided into triangles.
concepts.example: In quadrilateral ABCD, diagonal AC = 22 cm; BM is perpendicular to AC with BM = 3 cm and DN is perpendicular to AC with DN = 3 cm. Area(ABCD) = Area(ABC) + Area(ACD) = 1/2x22x3 + 1/2x22x3 = 33+33 = 66 cm2.

concepts.name: Area of a parallelogram and a rhombus
concepts.description: Dissecting a parallelogram into a rectangle of equal area to derive Area = base x height, and using the rhombus's diagonals to derive the special formula Area = half the product of the diagonals.
concepts.idea: A parallelogram can be cut and rearranged into a rectangle of equal area, giving Area = base x height for any side taken as base; a rhombus, being a parallelogram, also has Area = half x product of its diagonals.
concepts.rule: Drop a perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension) to get the height; cutting off the resulting triangle and moving it to the other end forms a rectangle of the same area, so Area of a parallelogram = base x height, and any side can be used as base with its matching height. A rhombus has all sides equal and diagonals that bisect each other at right angles; splitting it by its diagonals into 4 right triangles gives Area of a rhombus = 1/2 x product of the diagonals.
concepts.example: A parallelogram with base 7 cm and height 4 cm has area 28 cm2. A rhombus with diagonals 20 cm and 15 cm has area 1/2x20x15 = 150 cm2.

questions.a: Let the diagonals be AC and BD, meeting at O, with AC=d1, BD=d2, and OA=OC=d1/2, OB=OD=d2/2, meeting at right angles. Each of the 4 triangles, such as triangle AOB, has area 1/2x(d1/2)x(d2/2). Adding all 4 equal triangles: 4x1/2x(d1/2)x(d2/2) = 4x(d1xd2)/8 = (d1xd2)/2 = 1/2xd1xd2.

questions.q: A classmate says, 'Since a rhombus has 4 equal sides, its area must be side x side, just like a square.' Is this correct? Justify with an example.
questions.a: No. A rhombus's area depends on its height (or diagonals), not just its side length, because a rhombus can be squashed at different angles while keeping the same side length but changing its area; for example, a rhombus of side 10 cm can have height 8 cm (area 80 cm2) or height 6 cm (area 60 cm2) depending on its angle.

questions.q: Design a rhombus with area exactly 150 cm2 using two different pairs of diagonal lengths, and verify both give the same area.
questions.a: For example, diagonals 20 cm and 15 cm give 1/2x20x15=150 cm2. Also, diagonals 30 cm and 10 cm give 1/2x30x10=150 cm2. Both pairs give the required area of 150 cm2.

concepts.name: Area of a trapezium, and area units in real life
concepts.description: Deriving the trapezium area formula by dissection, and converting and estimating real-life areas using cm2, in2, ft2, m2, acres and km2.
concepts.idea: A trapezium's area can be found by dissection into a rectangle and triangles, or by joining two copies of it into a parallelogram, giving Area = half x height x sum of the parallel sides; real-world areas are measured and converted between several different units.
concepts.rule: For a trapezium with parallel sides a and b and height h, Area = 1/2 x h x (a+b). Two identical copies of the trapezium, one rotated 180 degrees and joined along a slanted side, form a parallelogram of base (a+b) and height h; the trapezium is exactly half of that parallelogram's area h(a+b). For units: 1 in = 2.54 cm, so 1 in2 = 2.54x2.54 = 6.4516 cm2; 1 ft = 12 in; 1 acre = 43,560 ft2; 1 km2 = 1,000,000 m2.
concepts.example: A trapezium with parallel sides 10 cm and 14 cm and height 6 cm has area 1/2x6x(10+14) = 72 cm2. An A4 sheet, 21 cm by 29.7 cm, has area about 624 cm2.

questions.q: Consider: (I) 1 acre equals 43,560 ft2. (II) 1 in2 equals 6.4516 cm2. Which is or are correct?
Derive the trapezium area formula Area = 1/2 h(a+b) by considering two congruent copies of a trapezium with parallel sides a and b and height h joined to form a parallelogram, explaining each step.
questions.a: Two copies of the trapezium, one rotated 180 degrees and joined along a slanted side, form a parallelogram whose base is a+b (the two parallel sides placed end to end) and whose height is still h, the same as the trapezium's height. The parallelogram's area is base x height = h(a+b). Since the parallelogram is made of exactly two copies of the trapezium, the trapezium's own area is half of this, giving Area = 1/2 h(a+b).

questions.q: A farmer wants to convert his 2-acre plot's area into square metres to compare with a neighbouring plot measured in m2. Is converting through square feet (acre to ft2 to m2) a reasonable approach? Justify.
questions.a: Yes, this is a reasonable approach, since acres and square metres are not directly related by a simple factor given in the chapter, but ft2 is a bridge unit whose relation to both acres (1 acre = 43,560 ft2) and metres is known, so converting via ft2 correctly gives the m2 value.

questions.q: Design a trapezium-shaped plot of land with area exactly 500 m2, choosing your own values for the two parallel sides and the height, and then state its area in acres (1 acre is about 4046.86 m2).
questions.a: For example, parallel sides 30 m and 20 m and height 20 m give Area = 1/2x20x(30+20) = 10x50 = 500 m2. In acres, this is about 500/4046.86, which is about 0.124 acres.
